![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14197370/assets/4408d1fcee1d168c6ab21ea53cf24845093bad9cc608299a36f0510c1636cc03.png)

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t},\,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14197370/assets/938f91220033a2174c011c1f8d65ff61e81e79b8af0ef718411169364c885418.png)

Consider the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2},$ where 

- ${C}_{1}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{1}(t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j$ for $t\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}],$ and

- ${C}_{2}$ is parametrized by ${r}_{2}(t)=t\,i+\,j$ for $t\in [-1,1].$

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ 

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is negatively oriented, and   

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & =-{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Notice that we have to take the line integral with a minus sign since our path is negatively oriented. 

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=i\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y & =-{∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & =-{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{-1}^{1}t\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2t}{2})\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{t}{2}-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2t]}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[\frac{\pi }{4}-0]-[-\frac{\pi }{4}-0] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $D$ be the region enclosed by the curve $C$ parametrized as
$r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡3t⟩$ for $t\in [0,2\pi ].$ The area of $D$ can be written as

$$
\text{Area}(D)={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})dA={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\boxed{}\,dt,
$$

where $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x.$ Determine the missing part of the equation.

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
{r}^{′}(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t+3\operatorname{sin}⁡3t,\,3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t⟩.
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡3t)\,dt.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Let $C$ be a simple, piecewise-smooth, closed, and positively oriented curve. Given that the line integral

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y
$$

 
represents the area of the region $D$ enclosed by any such curve in ${R}^{2},$ which of the following could be the functions $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)?$

I. $P(x,y)=-y-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y$

II. $P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=y$

III. $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=6{y}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
According to Green's theorem, if 

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,
$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

With that in mind, let's examine each pair in turn.

- Pair I gives the required area. In this case,
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1+\operatorname{sin}⁡y$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

- Pair II does *not* give the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0\ne 1.
$$

- Pair III gives the required area. Notice that
$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=0,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14197370/assets/86772e27f0a3226a608a1188fd8f58b9a8956f5f02fdbc5f9c2d29e2cef2a54c.png)

Use Green's theorem to find the area of the region enclosed by the curve 
$C$ parametrized as $r(t)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,i+3\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\,j$ 
for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0.$

Our simple, smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented, and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0-(-1)=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=-y$ and $Q(x,y)=0,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y=-{∮}_{C}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,i+12\operatorname{cos}⁡4t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate our line integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\text{d}u=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{∮}_{C}y\,dx & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\cdot (-6\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡4t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-18{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡2t(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-18{\int }_{1}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =18{\int }_{-1}^{1}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{u}^{3}{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =6({1}^{3}-(-1)^{3}) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$
